citation: Richardson, Jennifer C., Yukiko Maeda, Jing Lv & Secil Caskurlu. "Social presence in relation to students' satisfaction and learning in the online environment: A meta-analysis." Computers in Human Behavior 71 (2017): 402-417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2017.02.001.
discipline: Educational psychology / online-learning research (quantitative meta-analysis, CMC tradition)
thesis: A random-effects meta-analysis of 25 studies (1992-May 2015; N=3,862 for satisfaction, N=3,051 for perceived learning) pooling the CMC-tradition social-presence literature, finding a strong positive weighted-average correlation between social presence and satisfaction (r=0.56, SE=0.02, k=26) and between social presence and perceived learning (r=0.51, SE=0.05, k=26), each with substantial, systematic heterogeneity (I2=86.68% / 92.77%) explained in part by course length, discipline area, and (for satisfaction only) scale type and (for perceived learning only) target audience; positioned as the first quantitative synthesis of this literature.

sections.title: 1. Introduction (1.1-1.7)
sections.summary: Frames social presence as 'the ability to perceive others in an online environment,' tracing its lineage from social-psychology nonverbal-communication research (Argyle & Dean; Mehrabian) through Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) medium-salience coinage, Walther's CMC-era methodological critique, and Gunawardena's (1995) relocation of social presence to communicator perception. Table 1 catalogues 14 competing definitions (Short et al. 1976 through Garrison 2011); Table 2 catalogues self-report measurement instruments. Subsections 1.5.1-1.5.3 narratively survey social presence's reported relationships to satisfaction, to satisfaction/perceived-learning jointly, and to traditional graded performance (the last bracketed as too thinly studied to synthesize quantitatively). States three research questions on correlation strength and moderators for each of the two pooled outcomes.

sections.title: 2. Method (2.1-2.5)
sections.summary: Systematic search (1992-May 2015) across EBSCO, PsycINFO, ERIC, Education Full Text, dissertations, Google Scholar, the CoI website, and major conference archives yielded 98 candidate studies; inclusion criteria (fully online, higher-ed, social presence as theoretical frame, reportable quantitative correlation data) narrowed this to 25 studies (10 journal articles, 6 conference papers, 9 dissertations; N=3,862 for satisfaction across 19 studies, N=3,051 for perceived learning across 14 studies). Coded study characteristics: publication type, target audience, course length (6/8/16 weeks), discipline area, and social-presence scale used (Gunawardena & Zittle 1997; Richardson & Swan 2003; CoI survey; 'other'); inter-coder agreement 95.68%/96.43% before reconciliation to 100%. Used Fisher's r-to-z transformation and a random-effects model (inverse-variance weighting) to pool 52 total effect sizes (26 independent per outcome, after averaging dependent effect sizes from six studies with nested/repeated correlations, including Richardson & Swan 2003 itself). Heterogeneity assessed via Q, I2, and tau-squared; moderator analysis via CMA v2.0; publication bias checked via funnel plots, Orwin's Failsafe N, and Duval & Tweedie's Trim-and-Fill.

sections.title: 3. Results (3.1-3.3)
sections.summary: Satisfaction: weighted average r=0.56 (SE=0.02), Q(25)=187.64 p<.001, I2=86.68%, tau2=0.048. Significant moderators: course length (6wk r=0.48/k=3; 8wk r=0.72/k=2; 16wk r=0.53/k=9), discipline (Education r=0.42/k=7 < 'other' r=0.62/k=8, > Business r=0.32/k=3), and scale type (Richardson & Swan 2003 scale strongest at r=0.73/k=3 vs. Gunawardena & Zittle r=0.58/k=8, CoI r=0.62/k=4, other r=0.39/k=9); publication type and target audience non-significant. Perceived learning: weighted average r=0.51 (SE=0.05), Q(25)=345.77 p<.001, I2=92.77%, tau2=0.123. Significant moderators: course length (16wk r=0.58/k=11 > 8wk r=0.49/k=2 > 6wk r=0.45/k=3), discipline (Education r=0.42/k=7 < other r=0.62/k=8, > Business r=0.32/k=3), and target audience (certification/mixed r=0.59/k=9 > graduate r=0.47/k=5 > undergraduate r=0.35/k=4); scale type and publication type non-significant. Publication-bias diagnostics (funnel plots, Failsafe N=134 satisfaction / 82 perceived-learning, Trim-and-Fill) indicate minimal threat; imputed Trim-and-Fill estimate for perceived learning (r=0.613) would raise, not lower, the pooled estimate.

sections.title: 4. Discussion (4.1-4.4) & 5. Conclusion
sections.summary: Interprets both correlations as evidence social presence 'may very well predict' satisfaction and perceived learning, while stressing large unexplained heterogeneity. Course-length pattern read via Akyol & Garrison (2008)/Akyol, Vaughan & Garrison (2011): social presence 'develops' unevenly, affective expression waning as group cohesion rises. Discipline-area differences tentatively linked to hard/soft, pure/applied paradigm distinctions (Arbaugh, Bangert & Cleveland-Innes 2010) and science/humanities interaction-rate differences (Gorsky et al. 2010). Notes no two social-presence scales are equivalent; the Richardson & Swan (2003) scale showed both the strongest satisfaction moderation and the highest reliability among scales examined. States limitations (small k=26 per outcome limiting heterogeneity exploration; instructor behavior unexaminable, only 7/25 studies reported course-design elements; 57/98 originally identified studies excluded for missing statistical detail) and positions the study as the first quantitative synthesis of the CMC-tradition social-presence-and-outcomes literature.

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: organizing construct, defined study-wide as 'the ability to perceive others in an online environment'; the fixed predictor side of both pooled correlations; operationalized across 25 primary studies by four scale families (Gunawardena & Zittle 1997, Richardson & Swan 2003, CoI survey, single-study 'other' scales)

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: operationalized narrowly as self-report perceived learning (not measured achievement/retention/grades); pooled from 14 of 25 studies (30 extracted effect sizes, 26 independent); weighted average r=0.51 (SE=0.05, k=26), moderated by course length/discipline/target audience

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: operationalized as self-report satisfaction; pooled from 19 of 25 studies (28 extracted effect sizes, 26 independent); weighted average r=0.56 (SE=0.02, k=26), moderated by course length/discipline/scale type; framed with perceived learning as an 'affective' outcome pair per the authors' own prior methodological argument (Richardson, Maeda & Swan 2010)

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: named narratively in the introduction's literature survey (motivation, participation) as an outcome social presence has been shown to influence, but not itself extracted as a pooled effect size in this meta-analysis's quantitative apparatus

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.treatment: random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges & Vevea framework) pooling k=25 primary studies (1992-May 2015) via Fisher's r-to-z transformation and inverse-variance weighting; no single medium or immersion level contrasted -- the synthesized variation is among fully-online course designs (asynchronous/web-based CMC), not a media-comparison in the desktop-3D/IVR sense

readings.claim: Social presence is defined for this study as 'the ability to perceive others in an online environment,' a deliberately theory-agnostic gloss chosen to accommodate the field's competing definitions (catalogued in Table 1, Short et al. 1976 through Garrison 2011).
The weighted average correlation between social presence and satisfaction is r=0.56 (SE=0.02, k=26), with significant heterogeneity, Q(25)=187.64, p<.001, I2=86.68%.
The weighted average correlation between social presence and perceived learning is r=0.51 (SE=0.05, k=26), with significant heterogeneity, Q(25)=345.77, p<.001, I2=92.77%.

Course length, discipline area, and scale type significantly moderate the social-presence/satisfaction correlation; publication type and target audience do not; the correlation is equal for graduate and undergraduate courses.
Course length, discipline area, and target audience significantly moderate the social-presence/perceived-learning correlation; publication type and scale type do not.

Publication-bias diagnostics indicate minimal threat to the findings; the perceived-learning funnel's mild asymmetry, if corrected via Trim-and-Fill, would raise rather than lower the pooled estimate.

No two social-presence scales are equivalent; differing item coverage and reliability partly explain differing correlations, and the Richardson & Swan (2003) scale's higher reliability is read as consistent with, not merely coincidental to, its stronger satisfaction correlation.
This meta-analysis is the first attempt to quantify the common effect size and the disparity among effect sizes in the social-presence-and-outcomes literature.

concepts.term: moderator analysis (course length / discipline / audience / scale)

interlocutors.name: Same lead author as ped-sec-28 (Richardson & Swan, 2003)
interlocutors.role: self-citation lineage: this 2017 meta-analysis is the capstone quantification of the social-presence-predicts-outcomes claim ped-sec-28 first establishes on a single n=97 sample fourteen years earlier; ped-sec-28 is itself pooled as one of the 25 included primary studies, contributing multiple perceived-learning correlations, and the Richardson & Swan scale is the strongest satisfaction moderator (r=0.73) and most reliable scale examined

interlocutors.name: Short, John; Williams, Ederyn; Christie, Bruce
interlocutors.role: originators of social-presence theory and its medium-salience definition, the opening theoretical anchor of Table 1

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. (1995) and Gunawardena & Zittle (1997)
interlocutors.role: source of the communicator-perception revision of social presence and of the second most-used measurement scale (k=8 for satisfaction) among the 25 pooled studies; corresponds to ped-sec-25 in this cluster

interlocutors.name: Garrison, D.R., Anderson, T. & Archer, W. (1999)
interlocutors.role: source of the Community of Inquiry framework's definition of social presence (Table 1); corresponds to ped-sec-26 in this cluster

interlocutors.name: Tu, C.H. (2002a)
interlocutors.role: source of the SPPQ social-presence instrument (Table 2); corresponds to ped-sec-27 in this cluster

interlocutors.name: Walther, Joseph B.
interlocutors.role: CMC-era methodological critic of face-to-face/CMC comparison designs, cited in the introduction's theoretical lineage

interlocutors.name: Akyol, Zehra & Garrison, D. Randy
interlocutors.role: source of the 'social presence develops over time' interpretation used to explain the course-length moderator

interlocutors.name: Arbaugh, J.B., Bangert, A. & Cleveland-Innes, M. (2010)
interlocutors.role: source of the hard/soft, pure/applied paradigm explanation for the discipline-area moderator

interlocutors.name: Gorsky, P. et al. (2010)
interlocutors.role: comparator study finding higher science-course than humanities-course interaction rates, cited to interpret the discipline-area moderator

tensions.axis: social presence as technology-determined vs. social presence as psychologically/communicator-determined
tensions.note: The paper's introductory literature review sides, via Gunawardena (1995) and the CMC-era revisionists, with the communicator-determined pole, but the meta-analysis's own scale-type moderator finding (satisfaction correlations differ significantly by which scale is used) is read as evidence that measurement choices, not only underlying construct differences, drive some of the field's reported variation.

tensions.axis: perceived learning as a legitimate outcome vs. perceived learning as an inadequate substitute for traditional/graded performance
tensions.note: The authors explicitly defend perceived learning as often the outcome researchers intended to study (not a proxy failure), citing their own earlier argument (Richardson, Maeda & Swan 2010) that affective self-report measures are frequently the appropriate target, while acknowledging traditional-performance studies are too few to synthesize here.

tensions.axis: small-k meta-analytic power vs. comprehensive field synthesis
tensions.note: The authors register their own study's central limitation -- 26 effect sizes per outcome, drawn from a pool 57/98 originally identified studies had to exclude for reporting deficiencies -- as simultaneously a genuine constraint on generalizability and a call for improved field-wide reporting practices rather than a flaw unique to this synthesis.
